text: Two hangars, a U.S. airbase in Jordan, and a stack of satellite images that don't quite agree with each other. On July 9th, Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it fired 10 ballistic missiles at Muwafik Salty airbase and claims it destroyed hangars packed with American fighter jets. Jordan says almost none of that happened. So who's telling the truth?
Muwafik Salty sits about 100 kilometers east of Amman, out near Osroch.

The U.S. spent $143 million expanding it starting in 2019, and by 2026, it was hosting F-15s, F-22s, F-35s, and MQ-9 Reaper drones, reportedly the densest concentration of advanced U.S. strike aircraft anywhere in the Levant. This is one of America's most important forward operating bases in the entire Middle East. According to Iran's IRGC, this strike was the second phase of retaliation against the U.S., and Tehran said its aerospace force launched the missiles at 2.20 p.m. local time, targeting a U.S. command center and the Osroch base, claiming both were destroyed. They didn't stop there. The IRGC warned that if American strikes continue, other U.S. bases in the region will not be spared.

Jordan tells a very different story. Jordan's national news agency reported its air defenses intercepted eight of the incoming missiles, with no casualties or damage from the interceptions. Officials said the debris fell safely, with no damage on the ground. So, total destruction or a clean intercept.
Right now, both sides are sticking to their story. Here's where it gets interesting.

Independent analysts have been combing through Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, and some are flagging possible scorch patterns and structural anomalies around hardened hangars and flight line infrastructure at the base. But the resolution isn't great, and higher quality commercial imagery hasn't been released.
This isn't the first time this base has taken a hit, either.

Back in March, a U.S. TH-AD radar system at this same facility was confirmed damaged in an earlier exchange. This strike didn't happen in isolation. It was part of a four-country barrage that hit U.S. bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and Jordan within about 24 hours. If Iranian missiles really are reaching apron and hangar areas at one of the most heavily defended U.S. air bases in the region, that's a big deal for how survivable American air power actually is in this war. If they're not, it's a propaganda win dressed up as a military one. Either way, this is a story where the satellite images matter more than the statements.
